That’s why “The Inheritance” feels powerful only by its associations with an earlier tragedy. And maybe why the best way to approach the well-acted production is to test-drive it, by investing only in Part One. Lopez’s literary inspirations — “Howards End” and “Maurice” by E.M.
Lopez harnesses exhilarating forces, but then gets dragged by them, only to regain control for a moment, and then get yanked off his feet.
While “The Inheritance” as a whole is not as indispensable as its hype asserts, the first part, at least, delivers.

Ambitious though it is, “The Inheritance,” whose two installments run for well over six hours, is at once sentimental and static—far too much of it feels like a novel being read out loud from cover to cover—and the parts that work, poignant though they often are, fail to redeem those that don’t.

The Inheritance hereby joins that list.

Its social message aside, Lopez’s riveting two-part examination of how America’s gay men do – and sadly, don’t – learn lessons from previous generations (as well as each other) is a feat of unexpected theatrical daring, passion and beauty.

'The Inheritance' speaks to us on so many levels - politically, intellectually, and emotionally. If it rambles, it is an echo of our messy lives but it so clearly addresses the rootlessness that plagued the gay community for years.
Its timely themes make the story much greater than itself while telling an engrossing story of people we come to care about.
It is easily one of the best plays of the decade.
To put it bluntly, “The Inheritance” (which premiered at London’s Old Vic, transferred to the West End, and is now making its American debut) is the triumph of the fall theater season.

In the end, The Inheritance is a play whose cup runneth over in so many often glorious ways that almost every sip yields something — even if it might have been served just as well (or that much better) in a shorter, stronger pour.
The Inheritance ultimately proves to be more or less a high-grade soap opera.

The best advice about seeing The Inheritance on Broadway - which you definitely should if you're looking for a head-spinning, heart-rending theatrical experience - is to forget the hype surrounding it. And that won't be easy.
The playwright has made extraordinary use of 'Howard's End,' folding it into a modern context and adapting it to his needs.
There's so much here that's so wonderful that it's worth it to those with the stamina.
It's an Event, a worthwhile onerelevant, touching, and full of ghosts who deserve a hearing.
His is the story that makes Part One so complete, and it is the lack of his presence that makes Part Two less compelling.
Leaving the theater impressed and irritated is not just a set of genuinely conflicting feelings, it is also meant, finally, as very gay praise.

“The Inheritance” isn’t a great play or even a very good play, but Lopez’s opus is compellingly watchable in the way that old so-bad-they’re-good movies are: Finger-snapping one-liners and dramatic fireworks explode throughout as logic and character development are abandoned.

However, the current production flounders under Lopez’s overblown writing, which includes political polemics, moral debates and very long monologues about past events; and founders under Stephen Daldry’s direction, which too readily accommodates Lopez’s every whim.
Now at the Barrymore Theatre following a London premiere last year, this sprawling work is the most remarkable and heart-shattering new play on Broadway in recent memory.
'The Inheritance' truly surprises us, moment to moment, with its tender power and strong parallel story-telling.
Sitting in the audience, I was keenly aware that for many of us, gay and straight, hope was hard won, a tribute to those we lost.
For an endeavor so sweeping in scope, its findings are surprisingly narrow.
The hermetic, privileged circle tightens to a dot, and after nearly seven hours in the theater, we’re left with a play pointing eagerly and smugly at itself, waiting for a gold star.
The Inheritance is only an idea, no, an affectation of gay theatre.
It’s also melodramatically intense, angrily argumentative, unduly vulgar, egregiously overlong, and, while sprayed with strong laugh lines, emotionally overwrought.

cn.t: Lopez's ambitious 6+ hour epic about gay generations and AIDS divides critics: many praise its emotional power and importance, but others find it overlong and indulgent compared to the masterworks it evokes.

sg.ra: TickPick and Headout both name Center Orchestra rows E-J (TickPick: E-J; SeatPlan/Headout: F-O) as the prime zone at the Barrymore because the 1,058-seat house is shallow enough that the mezzanine overhang only kicks in at row K of the orchestra, leaving center rows F-J with an uncovered, forward sightline well-suited to the text-driven plays this house tends to book.

Headout and TickPick both warn against Orchestra rows A-C at the Barrymore specifically because the stage at this 1928 house sits high relative to the front rows — TickPick: 'rows A, B, and C are too close to the stage and might block your view'; Headout adds that 'seats closer to the stage may cause neck strain from looking upward.'

SeatPlan and TickPick both confirm the Barrymore mezzanine overhang begins at row K of the orchestra but isn't obstructive — SeatPlan: 'those sitting in the rear of the Orchestra section will notice that the stage feels impressively close'; the house's well-raked orchestra keeps sightlines intact even under cover, which matters because this is a 1,058-seat intimate-play house and losing the rear orchestra would shrink the good-seat pool significantly.

sg.vl: Elevated wide view, under premium pricing
sg.ra: SeatPlan directly names row A Center Front Mezzanine as the house favorite at the Barrymore — 'very popular thanks to its fantastic elevated position above the stage' — and both SeatPlan and TickPick emphasize the Barrymore's front mezzanine is only 5 rows deep (A-E, 196 seats), so even row E retains a wide, pitched view and benefits from the intimate 1,058-seat scale.

SeatPlan specifically praises the Barrymore rear mezzanine rake: 'a decent rake means even the back rows offer a surprisingly good look at the stage' and 'even in the far corner theatergoers won't feel too much strain to make out the stage.' The house's three-flights-up rear mezz is the trade-off for the small footprint, but the rake compensates for distance in a way deeper houses don't manage.

Headout and TickPick both flag the Barrymore's six box seats (three per side of the orchestra) and the orchestra rows D-E directly beneath them as compromised — Headout: 'seats under the Boxes in rows D and E a little restricted'; TickPick adds 'far Left and Right Orchestra and the outer corners of the Mezzanine can have reduced sightlines.' This is a specific quirk of the Barrymore's 1928 proscenium layout with built-in side boxes.
